case_analysis.focal_point: Whether Wisconsin’s interpretation of its unemployment-insurance “religious purposes” exemption unlawfully discriminates among religious organizations or excessively entangles the state in religious questions under the First Amendment.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Wis. Stat. § 108.02(15)(h)2. (the unemployment-insurance “religious purposes” exemption), as applied in light of the First Amendment (Religion Clauses: Free Exercise and Establishment/entanglement principles).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Catholic Charities Bureau and related Catholic entities argue that they qualify for Wisconsin’s statutory exemption because they are controlled by and operate as an arm of the Diocese’s religious ministry; Wisconsin’s contrary interpretation (requiring an organization’s activities to be more overtly or exclusively “religious,” or evaluating religiosity by the nature of services provided to the public) forces the state to draw theological lines and to rank religious missions, thereby creating unconstitutional entanglement and denominational discrimination. They further contend that denying the exemption burdens religious exercise by conditioning a benefit on adopting the state’s view of what counts as ‘religious’ work.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Wisconsin Labor & Industry Review Commission and the Department of Workforce Development maintain that the state supreme court’s construction is a permissible, neutral application of a state-law exemption designed to cover only organizations whose operations are for religious purposes as the statute uses that phrase; administering an exemption necessarily requires line-drawing and does not become unconstitutional merely because the claimant asserts religious motivation. They argue courts can deny religious tax/benefit exemptions without intruding into internal church governance, and that the petitioners’ First Amendment framing overstates the problem because the analysis focuses on statutory criteria rather than regulating doctrine or ecclesiastical decision-making.
key_precedents: United Coop. v. Frontier FS Coop., 2007 WI App 197

John Roberts.reasoning: The State’s strongest point remains that it must give content to the phrase “operated primarily for religious purposes,” and that some functional inquiry is inevitable to administer an unemployment-tax exemption; that argument has force, but it does not justify Wisconsin’s particular test, which (as described) turns on whether the ministry is overtly devotional or proselytizing and thus requires qualitative judgments about religiosity. Justice Kagan’s proposed path—allowing neutral, objective indicia such as ecclesial control, governance, and organizational integration—fits the statute’s administrability concerns while avoiding the entanglement and church-autonomy problems reflected in Hosanna-Tabor and Serbian Eastern Orthodox Diocese. Justice Thomas’s Larson point usefully highlights the risk that Wisconsin’s approach privileges certain forms of religious exercise, but I would rest the holding narrowly on the anti-entanglement/church-autonomy principle rather than expanding the doctrine unnecessarily. On that limited ground, the State may apply objective criteria, but it may not deny an exemption by second-guessing a church’s account of how service-oriented ministry constitutes religious purpose.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest contention is that the statute’s text—“operated primarily for religious purposes”—necessarily requires some examination of the organization’s activities; but under an original public meaning approach, the State may apply neutral, objective indicia of religious purpose and church control without arrogating to itself authority to decide whether a church’s ministry is “religious enough.” Wisconsin’s application, as described, crosses the First Amendment line by privileging ministries that look more overtly devotional and by forcing unemployment officials to engage in theological line-drawing, a classic Larson problem. Chief Justice Roberts’s emphasis on a narrow path is sound: the State can administer the exemption through objective criteria, but it cannot deny it by second-guessing the Church’s account of its own religious mission. Our Lady of Guadalupe reinforces that civil adjudicators lack competence to recharacterize religious functions, and that principle applies here even though the dispute arises in an unemployment-tax setting rather than an employment-discrimination suit.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The State’s strongest point is that the statute’s phrase “operated primarily for religious purposes” necessarily calls for some operational inquiry, and a State cannot administer an unemployment-tax scheme by accepting a purely self-declared religious label. But as Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes, Wisconsin’s application did not confine itself to neutral, objective indicia (governance, integration, formal affiliation); it pivoted on whether the ministry’s activities are overtly devotional or proselytizing, which compels officials to rank religious missions and invites denominational preference. Justice Thomas’s Larson framing reinforces that this is not merely line-drawing at the margins but a structural bias toward religions that express their faith through worship-like activity rather than service, and that constitutional defect is compounded by the practical consequence of routine “religiosity audits” by unemployment administrators. Precedents colleagues cited—Amos and the church-autonomy line (Hosanna-Tabor/Our Lady)—fit this case because they warn against government second-guessing how a church understands and carries out its religious mission, even in ostensibly secular regulatory programs.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The State’s best point is that “operated primarily for religious purposes” can’t be administered without looking at what an organization does, but that doesn’t justify Wisconsin’s apparent turn to a “devotional/proselytizing” test that pressures ministries serving vulnerable people to repackage service as worship to qualify. Chief Justice Roberts’s narrow approach is persuasive under my pragmatic lens: the State may use objective indicia like church control and organizational integration, but it may not rank religious missions or second-guess a faith’s understanding that charitable service is religious exercise. Justice Kagan’s emphasis on administrable, neutral criteria confirms this is not about letting the exemption swallow the rule; it’s about preventing entanglement and unequal burdens that predictably fall on certain traditions and on the people they serve. Justice Thomas’s Larson concern further underscores the real-world risk that “religious enough” screening will systematically privilege some denominations’ forms of practice over others, which is constitutionally intolerable.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The State’s best point is textual and administrative: “operated primarily for religious purposes” cannot be applied without some look at what an entity does, or else the exemption risks becoming boundless. But Chief Justice Roberts is right that Wisconsin’s described test goes past objective implementation into qualitative judgments about whether a ministry is sufficiently “overtly” devotional or directed to co-religionists—precisely the sort of entangling religiosity-ranking Amos cautioned against and that church-autonomy cases like Hosanna-Tabor/Our Lady of Guadalupe (as Justice Thomas and others note) reinforce. Under a pragmatic textualist approach, a workable middle ground is available: allow the State to use neutral, objective indicia (governance, church control, formal integration, stated mission) while forbidding administrators from recharacterizing service-oriented ministry as nonreligious because it lacks proselytizing trappings. Justice Sotomayor’s practical concern—that this regime pressures religious charities to “repackage” their work to satisfy state conceptions of religiosity—confirms the administrability and neutrality problems rather than answering them.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The State’s best point remains the textual one: the phrase “operated primarily for religious purposes” inevitably requires some inquiry into what an entity does. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan explain, Wisconsin’s approach goes beyond applying objective indicia and instead asks whether the ministry is “overtly” devotional or directed to co-religionists, which compels the State to rank religious missions and make theological judgments the First Amendment forbids. Justice Thomas’s Larson concern strengthens that conclusion: criteria privileging worship/proselytizing over service-as-religious-obligation risk denominational preference, not neutral administration. Hosanna-Tabor and Our Lady of Guadalupe confirm that civil authorities may not second-guess a church’s account of how it carries out its religious mission, even if the State may still apply the statute through neutral, objective factors (governance, church control, stated mission) without qualitative religiosity scoring.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The State’s best point is that administering “operated primarily for religious purposes” inevitably requires some inquiry into what an entity does, and an unemployment-insurance system cannot function if the exemption swallows the rule. But as Chief Justice Roberts persuasively frames it, Wisconsin’s application appears to hinge on whether the ministry is overtly devotional or proselytizing, which is not a neutral administrable line and instead invites unconstitutional theological ranking. Justice Barrett’s reliance on Amos strengthens the institutionalist concern: a regime that forces religious organizations to predict what officials will deem “religious enough” breeds entanglement and practical uncertainty, and Our Lady of Guadalupe cautions against civil recharacterization of how a church carries out its mission. A narrow holding—allowing objective indicia such as church control, governance, and stated religious mission while forbidding qualitative judgments about “religiosity”—respects precedent and limits disruption.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The State’s strongest point—that “operated primarily for religious purposes” requires some inquiry into actual operations—does not justify Wisconsin’s qualitatively devotional test, which converts a textual inquiry into a state evaluation of what counts as “religious” activity. Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan persuasively frame a narrower, text-respecting approach: the State may verify objective indicia (ecclesial control, governance, formal affiliation, stated mission) but may not deny the exemption because the ministry’s service is not overtly proselytizing. Justice Thomas’s Larson concern reinforces that Wisconsin’s criteria risk privileging certain forms of religious exercise over others, and our church-autonomy cases (Hosanna-Tabor/Our Lady) underscore why civil officials cannot recharacterize a church’s account of how service functions as religious mission. Precedent thus supports an as-applied holding against Wisconsin’s administration while leaving room for neutral application consistent with the statute’s original public meaning.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The State’s strongest point—that it must give content to “operated primarily for religious purposes” to keep the exemption administrable—has force, especially given the practical consequences for the unemployment-insurance system. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan stress, Wisconsin’s application goes beyond verifying neutral, objective facts and instead hinges on whether the ministry is “overtly” devotional or directed at co-religionists, which invites precisely the kind of theological line-drawing and denominational sorting the First Amendment bars. Justice Thomas’s Larson framing sharpens why this is not just entanglement in the abstract: a regime that privileges explicitly proselytizing models predictably disadvantages faith traditions that understand service to all as a core religious obligation. Under a procedurally fair, pragmatic approach, the State can use objective indicia (governance, church control, stated mission) but cannot condition benefits on officials’ qualitative judgments about how religious a ministry’s services look.

John Roberts.reasoning: Wis. Stat. § 108.02(15)(h)2. can be administered without the State undertaking a qualitative assessment of how “religious” an organization’s charitable works are, but Wisconsin’s interpretation—as described—appears to turn on whether the entity’s services are overtly devotional or proselytizing, effectively ranking religious missions and inviting precisely the kind of theological line-drawing the First Amendment forbids. Under Hosanna-Tabor Evangelical Lutheran Church & School v. EEOC, 565 U.S. 171 (2012), and its church-autonomy/entanglement lineage (including Serbian Eastern Orthodox Diocese), civil authorities may not decide religious questions by second-guessing a faith’s own understanding of its ministry. A narrow ruling is available: Wisconsin may apply neutral, objective criteria to define the exemption’s scope, but it may not deny it by evaluating the religiosity of petitioners’ functions in a manner that discriminates among religious organizations or excessively entangles the State in religious judgments.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Wis. Stat. § 108.02(15)(h)2. exempts employment by organizations "operated primarily for religious purposes" and controlled by a church; Wisconsin’s interpretation effectively conditions that exemption on the State’s assessment of whether the entity’s day-to-day works are sufficiently "religious" in character. That approach invites unconstitutional theological line-drawing and denominational preference by privileging religions whose ministries look more overtly devotional over those, like Catholic Charities, whose religious exercise is expressed through charitable service. The First Amendment forbids such denominational discrimination and state adjudication of what counts as “religious” activity. See Larson v. Valente, 456 U.S. 228, 244-46, 255 (1982), and Our Lady of Guadalupe Sch. v. Morrissey-Berru, 591 U.S. 732, 761 (2020).

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Wis. Stat. § 108.02(15)(h)2. exempts service performed for an organization operated primarily for “religious purposes,” and Wisconsin’s application effectively turns on whether the claimant’s ministry looks sufficiently “religious” to the State—an inquiry that invites theological line-drawing and preferential treatment among forms of religious expression. That approach risks the sort of denominational preference and ranking of religious missions the First Amendment forbids, because it conditions a statutory benefit on the State’s assessment of what counts as “religious” activity rather than on neutral institutional criteria. Under Larson v. Valente, government may not administer religion-based exemptions in a way that prefers some religious organizations over others, and this kind of religiosity-screening also creates the excessive entanglement concerns long recognized in the Court’s Religion Clause cases. Practical consequences reinforce the point: empowering unemployment officials to decide which ministries are “religious enough” predictably produces inconsistent, intrusive, and discriminatory administration.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Wisconsin’s application of Wis. Stat. § 108.02(15)(h)2. effectively conditions an otherwise available unemployment-insurance exemption on the State’s assessment of whether Catholic Charities’ services are sufficiently “religious” in character, inviting precisely the kind of intrusive line-drawing that risks excessive entanglement and denominational discrimination under the First Amendment. As Amos cautioned, the “religious character” of an activity is often not self-evident, and a regime that requires ongoing, case-by-case judgments about which charitable works count as religious pulls the State into evaluating religious mission and motivation rather than neutral administrative facts. That inquiry also burdens religious exercise by pressuring faith communities—especially those serving vulnerable populations through broadly available social services—to repackage their ministries to fit the State’s preferred model of religiosity. The Constitution permits neutral administration, but it does not permit the government to rank religious ministries or penalize churches for the organizational form and outreach they choose to carry out their faith commitments.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Wis. Stat. § 108.02(15)(h)2. turns on whether an organization is operated “primarily for religious purposes,” and Wisconsin’s interpretation—as applied—requires the State to appraise how “religious” the petitioner’s charitable works are by reference to the nature of the services and the population served. That kind of inquiry risks denominational discrimination and excessive entanglement because it forces civil authorities to decide which ministries count as sufficiently religious, a problem Amos warned against when it noted that the religious character of an activity is not self-evident and that probing it invites ongoing entanglement. A more workable and coherent reading is to focus on objective indicia of ecclesial control and integration (here, petitioner’s relationship to the Diocese) rather than second-guessing the Church’s account of how it carries out its religious mission, consistent with church-autonomy principles. On this record, the State’s application crosses the First Amendment line by conditioning a generally available statutory exemption on the government’s contestable judgments about religiosity.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Wis. Stat. § 108.02(15)(h)2. turns on whether an organization is operated “primarily for religious purposes,” and Wisconsin’s application effectively requires the State to judge the religiosity of Catholic Charities’ works by looking to how “overtly” religious the services appear and whom they serve—an inquiry the First Amendment does not tolerate. Our cases forbid government from second-guessing a religious organization’s own account of what its mission requires and from entangling itself in determining what counts as a religious function, see Hosanna-Tabor Evangelical Lutheran Church & School v. EEOC and Our Lady of Guadalupe School v. Morrissey-Berru. A construction that conditions an exemption on the State’s theological line-drawing risks denominational discrimination and excessive entanglement, and separation-of-powers principles counsel against inviting ongoing administrative supervision of religious ministries through unemployment-insurance enforcement. The statute can be applied using neutral, objective criteria (e.g., church control and corporate structure) without ranking religious missions, and Wisconsin’s contrary approach crosses the constitutional line.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Wis. Stat. § 108.02(15)(h)2. can be administered using neutral, objective criteria about organizational control and purpose, but Wisconsin’s interpretation goes further by requiring the State to assess whether the entity’s day-to-day charitable activities are sufficiently “religious” in the State’s view, which risks denominational discrimination and excessive entanglement. As Amos indicates, forcing a religious organization to “predict which of its activities a secular court will consider religious” burdens religious exercise and invites intrusive inquiries into the religious character of ministry work. That kind of searching evaluation of “religiosity” conflicts with the First Amendment’s church-autonomy/anti-entanglement principles reaffirmed in Our Lady of Guadalupe. Respect for history, tradition, and workable administration favors a rule that looks to the entity’s religious control and self-professed religious mission rather than judicial ranking of religious functions.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Wis. Stat. § 108.02(15)(h)2 turns on whether an entity is “operated primarily for religious purposes” and is controlled by a church or association of churches; Wisconsin’s construction, as described, effectively conditions the exemption on the State’s assessment of whether the organization’s day-to-day charitable works are sufficiently “inherently religious” rather than on the statutory and organizational criteria. That mode of decisionmaking risks denominational discrimination and excessive entanglement by requiring civil authorities to rank religious missions and parse theology to decide what counts as “religious” activity, a line the Court has warned is “hardly a bright one.” Corp. of Presiding Bishop v. Amos, 483 U.S. 327, 336 (1987). Consistent with Amos and church-autonomy principles reflected in Serbian Eastern Orthodox Diocese v. Milivojevich, 426 U.S. 696, 719–22 (1976), the First Amendment does not permit the State to penalize a church’s chosen organizational form for carrying out religious ministry by withholding an otherwise available exemption based on the State’s religiosity judgment.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Wis. Stat. § 108.02(15)(h)2. cannot be administered in a way that requires the State to evaluate how “overtly” religious an organization’s charitable services are or to rank religious missions based on the population served, because that invites precisely the kind of theological line-drawing and intrusive inquiry the First Amendment forbids. Under Corporation of the Presiding Bishop v. Amos, 483 U.S. 327 (1987), the Court recognized that government is not equipped to decide what duties or activities are “secular” versus “religious,” and exemptions that avoid such interference can be constitutionally permissible; Wisconsin’s approach moves in the opposite direction by conditioning exemption on the State’s assessment of religiosity. That method creates a serious risk of denominational discrimination and excessive entanglement, and it burdens religious exercise by forcing religious organizations to conform their ministries to the State’s view of what counts as “religious purposes.” A more procedurally fair and workable administration focuses on objective indicia of religious control and organizational status rather than adjudicating religious meaning in the organization’s day-to-day services.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether Wisconsin’s “religious purposes” exemption from unemployment-insurance coverage, as interpreted to deny the exemption to Catholic Charities because its services are not sufficiently religious in character, violates the First Amendment by entangling the state in religious line-drawing and/or discriminating among religious organizations based on their religious exercise.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Wis. Stat. § 108.02(15)(h)2. (the “religious purposes” exemption to unemployment-insurance coverage), and the First Amendment to the U.S. Constitution (Free Exercise and Establishment Clause / church-autonomy and entanglement principles).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Catholic Charities Bureau and affiliates argue that the Wisconsin Supreme Court’s interpretation forces the state to judge what counts as “religious” activity and to deny equal treatment to religious ministries that serve the public in non-proselytizing ways; they contend that this denominational or religiosity-based sorting both burdens religious exercise and creates unconstitutional entanglement, so the exemption must be applied without requiring the state to evaluate the religious content of charitable works (or the state’s interpretation must be rejected as unconstitutional).
case_analysis.respondent_position: Wisconsin agencies (LIRC/DWD) argue there is no cert-worthy split on the First Amendment issue and that states may administer religious exemptions by applying neutral statutory criteria without violating church autonomy; they contend that denying an exemption to entities asserting religious motivation is a routine, constitutionally permissible application of a tax/benefits exemption scheme that does not regulate internal church governance, compel religious practice, or create excessive entanglement.
key_precedents: United Coop. v. Frontier FS Coop., 2007 WI App 197

John Roberts.reasoning: The State’s strongest point is administrability: it must draw some line to apply a limited unemployment-tax exemption without swallowing the rule. But as Justice Kagan persuasively notes via Amos, when “the character of an activity is not self-evident,” Wisconsin’s case-by-case religiosity audit becomes both unworkable and constitutionally hazardous because it turns on whether a ministry looks sufficiently like worship or proselytizing. Justice Alito and Justice Kavanaugh reinforce that Wisconsin’s application effectively conditions eligibility on the State’s preferred markers of religious exercise (proselytizing, serving co-religionists), inviting entanglement and discrimination among faith traditions. A narrow as-applied disposition best protects institutional legitimacy: Wisconsin may use neutral, objective indicia to administer the exemption, but it may not deny it based on an assessor’s qualitative judgment that the charity’s service is not “religious enough.”

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The State’s strongest point is administrability: as Chief Justice Roberts notes, some line-drawing about “operated primarily for religious purposes” is unavoidable. But Wisconsin’s application does not confine itself to objective, text-based indicia (e.g., affiliation, governance, stated mission); instead it turns on an assessor’s judgment that Catholic Charities’ work is insufficiently religious because it lacks proselytizing or worship, the sort of theological appraisal civil magistrates lacked authority to make at the Founding. Justice Kagan’s invocation of Amos strengthens that conclusion by highlighting how such qualitative religiosity tests invite entanglement and discretionary supervision rather than neutral administration. Hosanna-Tabor and Our Lady of Guadalupe, though arising in a different posture, reinforce the same originalist principle: the Constitution withholds from the State jurisdiction to second-guess the religious character and means of a ministry’s exercise.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The State’s best point remains administrability—Wisconsin must draw some line to keep a limited unemployment-tax exemption from swallowing the rule—but that interest cannot justify the particular line Wisconsin drew here. As Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes, the denial turns on a qualitative judgment that Catholic Charities’ works are not "religious enough" because they lack worship or proselytizing, which is exactly the sort of intrusive, entangling inquiry Amos warned against, a point Justice Kagan reinforces with her administrability critique. Justice Thomas’s church-autonomy framing from Hosanna-Tabor/Our Lady of Guadalupe is not an exact doctrinal fit, but it strengthens the core constitutional intuition: civil officials may not sit in judgment of how a religious body chooses to express its faith through service. Textually, “operated primarily for religious purposes” can be administered through objective indicia (affiliation, governance, stated mission) without a state-imposed religiosity test, and Wisconsin’s contrary approach predictably pressures ministries to conform to the State’s preferred markers of faith.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The State’s strongest point remains administrability: it must draw some line to apply “operated primarily for religious purposes” within an unemployment-insurance regime. But as Justice Kagan and Chief Justice Roberts explain, Wisconsin’s as-applied approach does not rely on neutral indicia; it turns eligibility on whether the ministry’s service work is overtly devotional (proselytizing, worship-linked, co-religionist-directed), which both entrenches entanglement and effectively penalizes faith traditions that express religion through non-proselytizing service to anyone in need. Justice Thomas’s church-autonomy framing and Justice Alito’s invocation of Amos reinforce that the Constitution does not permit civil officials to appraise “religious enough” content as a condition of legal benefits, especially when the practical burden falls on vulnerable workers and beneficiaries if ministries are chilled or restructured. A narrow as-applied ruling can preserve the State’s programmatic interests by permitting objective criteria (affiliation, governance, stated mission) without ongoing supervision of religious practice.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The respondent’s best point is administrability: Wisconsin has to draw some line around “operated primarily for religious purposes,” and purpose inevitably requires some inquiry. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh emphasize, Wisconsin’s as-applied test doesn’t confine itself to objective, text-linked indicia (governance, affiliation, formal mission); it turns on a qualitative judgment that the service lacks sufficient religious content because it isn’t proselytizing or sectarian, which is exactly the entangling “religious enough” inquiry Amos warned becomes unworkable when the character of an activity is not self-evident. Justice Thomas’s church-autonomy framing from Hosanna-Tabor and Our Lady of Guadalupe is not perfectly on-point factually, but it reinforces the core constraint here: the State cannot sit in judgment of how a religious organization chooses to carry out its mission by demanding particular outward markers of religiosity. A narrow, text-coherent as-applied ruling remains available: Wisconsin may administer the exemption using neutral, ascertainable criteria, but it may not deny it based on evaluative comparisons of religious practice.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The State’s strongest point is administrability: it must draw some line around a statutory exemption limited to entities operated “primarily for religious purposes.” But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan both emphasize, Wisconsin’s as-applied approach does not rely on neutral, objective indicia; it denies the exemption only after officials decide the ministry’s works are insufficiently “religious” because they lack proselytizing, worship-like content, or sectarian limitation—exactly the kind of theological line-drawing that creates impermissible entanglement. Justice Thomas’s invocation of Hosanna-Tabor and Our Lady of Guadalupe, while arising in a different posture, reinforces the broader church-autonomy principle: civil authorities may not second-guess how a religious organization chooses to carry out its mission by demanding preferred outward markers of religiosity. A constitutionally permissible, textualist administration of “religious purposes” can be grounded in objective governance and affiliation facts; Wisconsin’s qualitative religiosity test, as applied here, crosses the First Amendment line.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The State’s best point remains administrability: it needs a workable way to confine the unemployment-tax exemption and cannot exempt every faith-affiliated nonprofit without collapsing the coverage scheme. But as Chief Justice Roberts explains, Wisconsin’s as-applied approach is not administrable in a constitutionally permissible way because it requires officials to decide whether Catholic Charities’ services are “religious enough” based on markers like proselytizing or serving co-religionists—an inquiry that predictably produces entanglement and de facto discrimination among faith traditions. Justice Kagan’s reliance on Amos reinforces that when “the character of an activity is not self-evident,” the State’s test devolves into discretionary, intrusive line-drawing rather than neutral, objective criteria (e.g., affiliation, governance, stated mission) that can serve the State’s interests. Justice Thomas’s church-autonomy framing (Hosanna-Tabor/Our Lady of Guadalupe) is not perfectly on-point factually, but it strengthens the principle that civil authorities may not sit in judgment of how a religious organization chooses to carry out its mission, which is exactly what Wisconsin’s test does here.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The State’s strongest point is that administering an exemption limited to entities “operated primarily for religious purposes” inevitably requires some line-drawing, and a neutral inquiry into purpose is not itself unconstitutional. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, Wisconsin’s application is not confined to objective indicia (governance, affiliation, corporate control, stated mission); it instead denies the exemption because the ministry’s service lacks proselytizing or sectarian restriction—an assessment that turns on officials’ judgments about what religious exercise should look like. That kind of qualitative “religious enough” test risks the entanglement and denominational preference the First Amendment’s original public meaning forbids, and the church-autonomy principles Justice Thomas highlights reinforce that civil authorities may not condition legal consequences on resolving such religious character questions. A narrow as-applied disposition remains available: Wisconsin may apply administrable, neutral criteria, but it may not deny this exemption based on an assessor’s evaluation of the religious content of charitable works.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The State’s best point remains that it is defining the scope of a generally applicable unemployment-tax exemption, not prohibiting Catholic Charities’ work; but that characterization collapses once eligibility turns on the State’s qualitative judgment about whether the charity’s service is “religious enough.” Chief Justice Roberts’s framing crystallizes the procedural-fairness problem: Wisconsin’s criteria (proselytizing, worship-linked activity, serving co-religionists) require officials to appraise religious meaning and thereby pressure ministries to modify practice to fit state-preferred markers. Justice Kagan’s reliance on Amos reinforces the practical consequences and administrability defect—when “the character of an activity is not self-evident,” the State’s case-by-case religiosity inquiry predictably yields inconsistent and discriminatory outcomes across faith traditions that express religion through service rather than overt devotional speech. On my pragmatic view, the Constitution permits neutral, objective indicia to administer the exemption, but forbids this as-applied regime that functionally penalizes certain religious modalities and entangles the State in religious evaluation.

John Roberts.reasoning: Wis. Stat. § 108.02(15)(h)2., as applied, turns the exemption on a state tribunal’s assessment of whether Catholic Charities’ works are “sufficiently religious” (e.g., proselytizing or worship), inviting the very kind of governmental line-drawing about religious character that the First Amendment cautions against. Under Hosanna-Tabor Evangelical Lutheran Church & Sch. v. EEOC, the Constitution protects a religious organization’s right to define and carry out its mission without intrusive state judgments about what counts as religious function, and Wisconsin’s approach risks excessive entanglement by conditioning legal status on that judgment. A narrow ruling is available: Wisconsin may administer its unemployment scheme, but it cannot deny the statutory exemption based on qualitative evaluations of religiosity that discriminate among religious ministries depending on how they express their faith in public service. Given the significant constitutional avoidance concerns and the institutional interest in keeping government out of theological assessments, the application here violates the First Amendment.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The First Amendment’s text forbids laws “prohibiting the free exercise” of religion and bars governmental structures that require civil officials to decide what religious activity is “sufficiently” religious; Wisconsin’s interpretation of Wis. Stat. § 108.02(15)(h)2. does exactly that by conditioning the exemption on the State’s assessment of the religious character of Catholic Charities’ works. Under Hosanna-Tabor Evangelical Lutheran Church & Sch. v. EEOC and Our Lady of Guadalupe Sch. v. Morrissey-Berru, the Constitution protects church autonomy by limiting state inquiry into matters of faith, doctrine, and the internal religious mission, and Wisconsin’s proselytizing-centered line-drawing invites precisely the entanglement those cases reject. Moreover, denying a generally available exemption based on the State’s view that a religious ministry is insufficiently religious resembles unconstitutional discrimination among religious organizations and burdens religious exercise in the manner condemned in Trinity Lutheran Church of Columbia, Inc. v. Comer. Consistent with textual limits on state power and the original meaning that civil authorities may not sit in judgment of religious orthodoxy, the exemption must be applied using neutral, readily ascertainable criteria rather than evaluative theological tests.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Wis. Stat. § 108.02(15)(h)2. turns on whether an entity operates “for religious purposes,” and Wisconsin’s interpretation—denying the exemption because Catholic Charities’ works are not sufficiently “religious in character”—requires the State to make fine-grained judgments about what counts as religious activity. That kind of governmental line-drawing risks the very “searching case-by-case analysis” and “ongoing government entanglement in religious affairs” the Court warned about in Corporation of Presiding Bishop v. Amos, 483 U.S. 327, 343–344 (1987) (Brennan, J., concurring), and it pressures religious organizations to structure their ministries to satisfy the State’s conception of religiosity. Whatever Wisconsin’s administrative interests in uniform unemployment-insurance coverage, the First Amendment does not permit conditioning a religious exemption on an official assessment of whether a religiously motivated charity is “religious enough,” which invites discrimination among religious ministries based on how they choose to serve the public.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Wis. Stat. § 108.02(15)(h)2., as applied here, turns the exemption on whether Catholic Charities’ social services are “sufficiently religious,” effectively requiring state officials to police the religious character of ministry work and disadvantaging faiths that serve through non-proselytizing charity. That kind of religious line-drawing risks unconstitutional entanglement and unequal treatment among religious organizations based on the manner of their religious exercise, contrary to the church-autonomy principles recognized in Hosanna-Tabor and related cases limiting governmental inquiry into what is “religious.” A more administrable, constitutionally safer approach is to apply neutral, objective criteria (e.g., affiliation and organizational purpose) without evaluating the religiosity of the services themselves, avoiding burdens that will predictably fall hardest on vulnerable workers and beneficiaries caught in prolonged church–state disputes. Because Wisconsin’s interpretation invites ongoing monitoring of religious practice and discriminates among religious ministries, it violates the First Amendment.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Wis. Stat. § 108.02(15)(h)2., as applied here, turns the exemption on whether Catholic Charities’ service activities are “sufficiently religious,” which necessarily forces state decisionmakers to draw contested lines between religious and secular conduct and to privilege proselytizing forms of ministry over others. That kind of inquiry risks the very entanglement problem Justice Brennan identified in Corporation of the Presiding Bishop v. Amos, where “the character of an activity is not self-evident,” and determining whether it is “religious” invites ongoing, case-by-case governmental assessment of religious meaning. Whatever room a State has to define the scope of a benefits exemption, this interpretation is not especially workable or coherent because it requires administrators to evaluate religious content rather than apply administrable, neutral criteria tied to organizational status or church control. On this record, the First Amendment is better served by construing or applying the exemption without a religiosity test that conditions equal treatment on the perceived religious character of charitable works.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Wis. Stat. § 108.02(15)(h)2. exempts employment by entities organized and operated "primarily for religious purposes," and Wisconsin’s application here turns on an assessor’s judgment that Catholic Charities’ works are not sufficiently “religious” because they are offered without proselytizing or sectarian limitation. That sort of state line-drawing about what religious exercise must look like invites the very entanglement and intrusion into church governance the First Amendment forbids, as reflected in Hosanna-Tabor and Our Lady of Guadalupe’s insistence that civil authorities may not second-guess how religious organizations carry out their ministries. Conditioning equal treatment on whether a ministry’s charitable service appears “religious enough” risks discrimination among faiths and forms of religious exercise, and it pressures religious entities to alter their practice to satisfy the state’s preferred markers of religiosity. The Constitution permits neutral, administrable criteria, but not an inquiry that effectively adjudicates the religious character of a ministry’s works to deny the exemption.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Wis. Stat. § 108.02(15)(h)2., as applied here, appears to require state officials to determine whether Catholic Charities’ service ministries are “sufficiently religious,” a kind of religious line-drawing that risks unconstitutional entanglement and discrimination among religious organizations based on the form of their religious exercise. Under Corporation of the Presiding Bishop v. Amos, the Court has cautioned that governments are not well equipped to classify duties or activities as “secular” versus “religious,” because that inquiry becomes an intrusive assessment of religious belief and practice. Even accepting the State’s interest in administrable exemption criteria, the Wisconsin Supreme Court’s interpretation is not practically workable without probing religious character, and it burdens religious entities that serve the public in non-proselytizing ways, contrary to neutrality principles reflected in this Court’s Free Exercise cases. A narrower, history-and-tradition-consistent application of the exemption that avoids doctrinal evaluations is required to protect First Amendment church-autonomy and to maintain a predictable, restraint-based rule.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Wis. Stat. § 108.02(15)(h)2 turns on whether an entity is “operated primarily for religious purposes,” and the Wisconsin Supreme Court’s application—requiring officials to assess whether Catholic Charities’ services are sufficiently “religious” (e.g., proselytizing, targeting co-religionists)—invites the State to make qualitative judgments about religious exercise. That kind of religious line-drawing risks unconstitutional entanglement and discrimination among religious organizations based on how they manifest their faith, contrary to the church-autonomy and anti-entanglement principles reflected in Hosanna-Tabor Evangelical Lutheran Church & Sch. v. EEOC, 565 U.S. 171 (2012). While the State may administer neutral benefit schemes, the First Amendment forbids inquiries that effectively rank religious ministries by “religiosity” rather than applying objective criteria that avoid doctrinal appraisal. Given that the statutory standard as construed requires precisely that appraisal, the denial of the exemption to Catholic Charities is likely unconstitutional as applied.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Wis. Stat. § 108.02(15)(h)2, as applied here, appears to require the State to evaluate whether Catholic Charities’ service ministries are “sufficiently religious” based on factors like proselytizing and overt religious content, which risks the kind of governmental entanglement and interference with a church’s mission that the First Amendment prohibits. Under Hosanna-Tabor Evangelical Lutheran Church & School v. EEOC, the Court emphasized that civil authorities may not intrude into questions that bear on a religious organization’s faith and mission; Wisconsin’s line-drawing about what counts as a “religious” charitable purpose presses the State into theological assessment. That inquiry also creates unequal treatment among religious organizations by privileging ministries that look more “church-like” over those whose religious exercise is expressed through non-proselytizing service, raising Free Exercise and equal-protection-like concerns about discriminatory administration. A more administrable, fair approach consistent with Jones v. Wolf would rely on objective, neutral indicia (e.g., organizational affiliation and stated religious mission) rather than adjudicating the religiosity of day-to-day services.
